subject: dominic-fike
research_tasks: Research log (2026-10-31, first run, mode create, empty baseline, no research notes or prior evidence). Opened 24 sources (one unavailable). Read in full: Interview Magazine with Curry Barker (S01), British GQ 2022 (S02), Guardian 2023 (S03), Evening Standard 2023 (S04), NME 2020 (S05), Pigeons & Planes 2019 (S06), Blackbird Spyplane 2023 (S07), Variety 2021 (S08). Transcribed: the Apple Music/Zane Lowe Naples film (S09, 49 minutes of YouTube captions plus seven segments re-transcribed from audio with Whisper medium.en), the 2026 Pigeons & Planes video (S10, 17 minutes, Whisper small.en; no captions existed), and the full Armchair Expert episode (S11, about 80 minutes of conversation, Whisper small.en plus eight segments re-transcribed with medium.en). About 45,000 words of transcript in all; copies are in ~/.cache/9takes-research/dominic-fike/ (not the repo). Secondary checks: S12-S20, S22-S25. Evidence was gathered and catalogued before a type was chosen; Types 7, 6, 9, 4, 3, 8 and 2 were each tested against it. Outcome: status ready, profile_format standard (his public record runs from 2018 and is deep; he does not qualify as an open case). Leading read Type 7 at medium confidence; Type 6 is the strongest alternative; wing left unknown. Risks: sensitive_allegations is true (criminal record, addiction and withdrawal accounts, drug use he says began at ten, parents' addiction and incarceration, domestic violence, Hunter Schafer's infidelity account, his own account of an earlier infidelity, siblings' legal and treatment matters, a young child), so the six-role jury applies. contested_typing is false: no published typing was found to contest, and the Six alternative is argued in type_hypothesis; a reviewer may escalate.

Accuracy check (2026-10-31). How To Quit Smoking was released October 30, 2026 on Columbia (15 tracks, about 40 minutes; first announced for October 9; singles 'Wallflower' August 28, 'Small Town' September 18, 'Pangea' October 19) (S15-S17, S19). 'Babydoll' reached No. 10 on the Hot 100 dated October 24, 2026, his first top 10 (S15); Wikipedia's artist page still says No. 16. The Comedy Tragedy Parody Tour began in Australia in December 2025 after a break; the North American leg ran August 15-September 30, 2026, alongside support dates for Tame Impala (S18, S17). He confirmed a son, Rocket, on April 7, 2026 (S10). He said in December 2025 he was in a relationship (Wikipedia; not opened at source; do not print). Euphoria season 3 aired in 2026 (coverage not opened reports an April 12 premiere); whether his filmed scenes aired is unverified (C17). The backlog note's 'Europe tour Feb 2027' was not verified and must not be printed; check his site before any mention. Turns 31 on December 30, 2026; use his birth year with absolute dates rather than an age where possible.

Drafting guidance. Standard profile, Type 7 leading at medium confidence; set enneagram: 7, type: ['celebrity'] per site convention, published: false. Strong verified hooks (choose one): (a) the motel scene: on a promotional shoot in July 2023 Zane Lowe took him back to the Naples motel room his family lived in, and five minutes in he said 'this is too much, should we go to fucking beach' and went swimming (S09 32:50-33:50, observed); (b) the Forest of Avalon told three times over six years, ending with 'I wanted Alice in Wonderland... I wanted there to be some sort of danger' (S06, S07, S11); (c) the 'Transformers band-aid' over a 'gash' (S11, verify audio). The central insight: hardship told as adventure is not denial of the facts (he states them flatly) but a refusal to stay inside them; it explains the costly choices (shrooms before the audition, cocaine on house arrest when 'trapped' and 'bored', yacht money, relapses) and his own late insight that success was a band-aid. Keep 'What is Dominic Fike's personality type?' with an answer of at most 60 words, e.g. 'Most likely a Type 7, held at medium confidence: his repeated move is to leave pain for stimulation and recast it as fine. Type 6 is the serious alternative, because he names safety as a lifelong problem.' Put the Six case beside the Seven case with his own security quotes (C20, C21, C24) and the discriminator (C16, C06, C11). Show what the type does not explain: the mother's 'quiet observer' (C23), not approaching people (C22), loyalty (C24), the grief he describes alone (C37). Durable spine: the 2019-2026 pattern. Use 'Babydoll' at No. 10 and the October 30, 2026 album only as the reason people are searching, dated. Target 2,000-3,500 words.

Quotation cautions. (a) S09 is YouTube auto-captions; quote only passages re-transcribed from audio (listed in its locator) or check the audio first. 'I had a really hard time sitting still in my own skin... I had my own distractions... drinking' is ZANE LOWE, not Fike. The mother passage is attributed by context; confirm on video and call her 'his mother'. (b) S10 and S11 are Whisper machine transcripts without speaker labels; several vivid lines in S11 belong to Dax Shepard or Monica Padman ('jumping off the second floor into the pool', 'arousal setting was set way too high', 'That's the great thing about coke. It makes you optimistic', the bar-mirror story). Confirm the voice on audio for 'I had a good time in jail' (00:42:30), 'I never extend that care to myself' (00:23:50; may be Shepard), 'self-defense mechanism' (01:02:30) and 'piece of shit... self-protection' (01:18:30). (c) The Los Angeles Times interview (Mikael Wood, July 6, 2023) was not opened; cite its quotes 'as reported by TheWrap' (S13). (d) The 'Babydoll' Instagram caption is quoted from Wikipedia (S24); verify before printing. (e) The British GQ piece (S02) is a US GQ interview by Samuel Hine; 'spin into a positive' and 'yachts' are the writer's words; 'Eric Clapton–funded' is GQ's attribution of the Antigua centre. (f) Variety 2021 says he was sober during season 2 filming; he later said he was using then. Present both with dates, not as a lie. (g) The 'Whatever I do, I do too much of it' Guardian headline paraphrases him; the body quote is about drugs. (h) Interviewers misstate the arrest ('punched a cop'); his account is that he tripped or knocked down an officer he thought had drawn a gun (later: a taser). (i) Do not quote the Complex/Variety Sundance lines as Variety without opening Variety's video. (j) Keep his profanity as spoken; do not tidy disfluent machine-transcribed speech into cleaner sentences he did not say.

Sensitivity. Addiction and recovery: use his words, dated; no diagnostic labels, no speculation about current sobriety or risk; do not make the benzodiazepine withdrawal crisis or 'near-death' drug line the hook or the ending, and do not connect him to Angus Cloud's death. Childhood: drug use from age ten, parents' heroin use, his mother's incarcerations and the stepfathers' violence are his accounts; state them briefly and without causal claims that trauma made his type. Family privacy: do not name his sister, and do not detail siblings' arrests, treatment or custody matters or his father's sentence; 'his mother' and 'his younger brother' suffice beyond what he has made central (his brother at the 2016 arrest). Relationships: attribute Hunter Schafer's account of infidelity to her, give his stated reason for the split (codependency, July 2023), note no response was found, and do not speculate about lyrics; do not name the earlier partner he discussed on Armchair Expert or repeat that story beyond 'he has described cheating in an earlier relationship before his 2020 rehab' if needed at all; do not report his December 2025 relationship. Child: only his words; never name or speculate about the child's mother. The 'yacht with 15-20 women' anecdote happened while he was dating Schafer; use with care or not at all. Criminal record: battery on a police officer (pleaded guilty), house arrest, failed drug test, county jail; avoid 'assaulted' as an unattributed verb.

Follow-ups before or at the next refresh: (1) confirm whether his Euphoria season 3 scenes aired (HBO credits, a reliable recap; the Men's Journal page S21 was CAPTCHA-blocked); (2) open the 'Babydoll' Instagram caption or a report quoting it; (3) find the Los Angeles Times interview of July 6, 2023; (4) look for on-record testimony from people who knew him before 2018 (Naples collaborators, his manager Reed Bennett, Kevin Abstract's June 2025 Zach Sang interview about Geezer) and the 2020 New York Times Presents documentary; (5) check How To Quit Smoking interviews from the release week (Apple Music, podcasts) for how he describes quitting and the Tay-K closer; (6) recheck the 'Babydoll' chart run and any 2027 tour dates. A Six-versus-Seven settle signal for a refresh: in a sober, settled period (fatherhood, a hit), does he describe what steadies him as people, preparation and stability he can count on (Six), or as new projects, motion and keeping things light (Seven)?

Draft stage (2026-10-31). Wrote a standard Type 7 profile (about 3,500 words, published: false). Re-verified quoted passages against cached copies: re-transcribed seven Zane Lowe film clips (motel, security, codependency, mother, closing chapter, ride, social) and three Armchair Expert windows (01:02:36-01:03:00, 01:18:26-01:19:10, 00:50:48-00:51:20) with Whisper medium.en; checked printed quotes in GQ, the Standard, the Guardian, NME, P&P 2019, Blackbird, Variety 2021 and Interview against the cached pages. Not printed because speaker turns stay ambiguous in machine transcripts: 'self-defense mechanism', 'a little bit of that self-protection', 'I never extend that care to myself'. Corrected: 'trying to cheat a connection' is Zane Lowe's phrase, which Fike agreed with. Still unverified and kept out of the article: whether his Euphoria season 3 scenes aired (C17 removed from the draft inventory; S20/S21 retained), the 'Babydoll' Instagram caption (C36 removed; S24 retained for the re-release date), the Los Angeles Times original (TheWrap attribution kept). Printed on transcript turn context only, without listening: 'I had a good time in jail' (C65), 'These dudes start flying from California' and 'Al Capone' (C66), the mother's identification in the Lowe film (C23); an audio or video check is the next verification step. sources.title: Dominic Fike Tells Curry Barker Why He Can't Sit Still
sources.speaker: Dominic Fike in conversation with filmmaker Curry Barker (a friend and self-described fan), Interview Magazine
sources.date: 2026-10-07 (published; conversation dated Tuesday, August 11, 2026, Sherman Oaks, during tour rehearsals)
sources.locator: Q&A, opening exchange (Courtyard Marriott, vegan, "sacrifice chickens and cows"); answer on picking songs ("I have the metrics", Reed Bennett, "White Keys" found on an old phone); answer on fans vs. art ("Back in 2019, when I got a deal, I was only thinking about what other people wanted", meditation analogy, "White Keys" written drunk); answer on money and the kid ("it's always you", "I was lazy back then"); "write a song in 10 minutes, but I was just trying to flex"; "I forgot where we were going"; pressure answer ("There's no pressure in the studio... The pressure drops away if you're doing it right"); "big ass boat"; "They know I can be finicky with dates"; acting answer ("you don't want to be in people's faces too much", Dune press run); "I've never been the type of guy to intrude on anybody's shit. That's why I do all this shit myself. That's why I'm bad at asking girls out."
sources.excerpt: "Back in 2019, when I got a deal, I was only thinking about what other people wanted." [...] "Sometimes you get influenced by other people, but you always bring it back." [...] "I would write a song in 10 minutes, but I was just trying to flex." [...] "There's no pressure in the studio. And if you're really songwriting, you don't have the space to feel any of that. It's like running." [...] "They know I can be finicky with dates." [...] "I always believe you don't want to be in people's faces too much." [...] "I've never been the type of guy to intrude on anybody's shit. That's why I do all this shit myself. That's why I'm bad at asking girls out."
sources.context: Friendly peer conversation recorded during rehearsals for the fall 2026 tour, published three weeks before How To Quit Smoking. Barker flatters him throughout; Fike drifts between jokes (Texas age-verification, porn) and serious answers and admits losing the thread. Also says he is 'trying to be vegan', that his manager shows him streaming metrics ('As much as I hate to see it'), that he has 'more time to make music' now with a kid and money, and that he got 'lucky' on acting. The page title ('Why He Can't Sit Still') is the editors', not his words. Interview's October 30, 2026 Sound Advice column reprints pull quotes from this conversation and is not an independent source.

sources.excerpt: "there's not a single difficult topic – not his family nor incarceration nor addiction – that Fike can't spin into a positive. (He describes jail, for example, like a sabbatical: 'It really was just a year off to focus on myself.')" [...] "I was going through so much then, and I was heavily addicted to so many drugs." [...] "Whatever happened was cool." [...] "I'm trying to go crazy. I'm trying to be like Lindsay Lohan. I'm trying to be annoyed at paparazzi and shit." sources.title: 'Whatever I do, I do too much of it': the troubled rise of Dominic Fike (The Guardian)

sources.locator: Paragraphs 1-3 (jail as "purgatory"; "I was not doing too well"); "Idle hands are the devil's work"; industry-plant paragraph ("All I know is I'm pushing forward regardless of expectation", Harry Styles "well-oiled machine"); McCartney cover; childhood paragraph; "Whatever drug I would do, I'd do too much of it"; Euphoria sober coach ("I was more like … psyched!"); Sunburn reception (peaked No 30 US); "I had an unhealthy relationship with releasing music"; "If I have some coke, everyone around me feels it"; Bieber/tequila "I wish I could do that... But I fucking can't do it: I tried."
sources.excerpt: "Whatever drug I would do, I'd do too much of it – to [the point of] a near-death, surreal experience. I just kind of thought that was how you did drugs – to go all the way there without dying," he says. [...] "I was using at the time, but I wasn't worried. I was more like … psyched!" [...] "Idle hands are the devil's work … the cool part about the label thing is that it helped me keep my shit together in jail." [...] "All I know is I'm pushing forward regardless of expectation." [...] "I wish I could do that … be this huge pop star and have a drink and not have a bunch of anxiety. But I fucking can't do it: I tried."
sources.context: UK tour preview two months after Sunburn, which the writer says underperformed commercially. The headline phrase 'Whatever I do, I do too much of it' is a headline paraphrase; the quoted sentence in the body is about drugs. The piece calls his custody 'prison' in one place; he served county jail time (S06, S05). Written two months after Angus Cloud's death, which the writer mentions; Fike does not comment on it in the piece.

claims.claim: Type synthesis (interpretation): the most repeated, cross-context behavior in the record from 2019 to 2026 is a three-part move when pain or limitation appears: leave it for stimulation or open space (the Forest of Avalon, cocaine when 'trapped' and 'bored', the motel exit to the ocean, 'anywhere else but in my body'), recast it as fine or good (jail as a 'year off' and 'a good time', relapses 'all good', addiction 'made me better'), and keep moving ('go-mode', 'tiles under my feet', impatience to release). This is the Seven pattern of avoiding pain and limitation by keeping options and experience open.

claims.inference: Grounded in self-report, three journalists' independent observations and one filmed scene, across sober and using periods. It explains costly choices (the audition, the failed drug test, yacht spending, relapses) better than image (Three) or security (Six).
claims.alternative: Addiction and childhood trauma produce escape and minimization in every type; promotional interviews reward lightness; and the mother's 'passive, quiet observer', his reluctance to approach people, and his loyalty fit Six or Nine. See type_hypothesis.

claims.claim: He describes both parents as drug addicts, on heroin.

claims.inference: Consistent in outline across 2019-2025 and five interviewers. This is circumstance, not motive: any type argument has to show what he does with this history, not cite the history as evidence.
claims.alternative: The details shift by telling (the father 'rode off' on his brother's scooter in GQ; 'stealing his brother's electric scooter' in the Standard). Trauma of this kind produces escape, vigilance or numbing in people of every type. Sensitive: no clinical or causal language; never use it as the hook's punchline.

claims.claim: His mother was in and out of jail and his father was largely absent.

claims.inference: Consistent across P&P 2019, Guardian 2023 and GQ 2022 accounts.
claims.alternative: Circumstance, not motive; stated without causal claims.

claims.inference: Blackbird Spyplane, July 2023 ("when I was homeless and 16 and people would pay me for features so I could buy motel rooms and food").
claims.alternative: Single self-report.

claims.claim: Tasbeeh Herwees (Pigeons & Planes, 2019) wrote that he lists the facts of his life "with no sense of drama" and that his childhood, he says, "was otherwise full of adventure."
claims.passage: "These are facts of his life he lists with no sense of drama. His childhood, he says, was otherwise full of adventure."
claims.inference: Independent journalist observation of affect (see C07).
claims.alternative: One writer, one reporting period.

claims.claim: In 2025 he explained the Forest of Avalon trips: every time he left the house he wanted "Alice in Wonderland" and "some sort of danger."
claims.passage: "So every time I left the house, it was like, let's get into it. I wanted Alice in Wonderland... Every time. I wanted there to be some sort of danger."
claims.inference: Whisper medium re-transcription (aeseg-alice, 00:27:50-00:29:40) confirms wording; the ellipsis marks a host interjection ("Yeah, yeah"). The next line ("our arousal setting...") is Shepard's, not Fike's.
claims.alternative: Leaving a chaotic house for the woods is ordinary adolescence. Dax Shepard reads it as a high arousal set-point produced by chaos (trauma physiology, not type). The 2025 telling is shaped by a host who shares the story.

claims.claim: The Forest of Avalon told in 2019 ("imagine that it was another place") and 2023 ("like we'd traveled through time").
claims.passage: As young teenagers, he and his friends biked to a patch of land they called the Forest of Avalon to smoke weed and, in his 2019 words, "imagine that it was another place." In 2023 he said it was "like we'd traveled through time."
claims.inference: Same story told to different interviewers years apart (Blackbird: "as 14 year olds").
claims.alternative: Ordinary adolescence; trauma reading in C57.

claims.claim: In 2025 he called it "literally an undeveloped lot" and said his home was small and its problems "so present."
claims.passage: he described it plainly ("It was literally an undeveloped lot. It was just a lot that had not yet turned into a Ritz") and then explained why it mattered: "my home was small and the problems were so present."
claims.inference: Whisper medium re-transcription (aeseg-alice).
claims.alternative: Host-shaped conversation; Shepard shares the story.

claims.claim: Dax Shepard offered a trauma explanation: people raised in chaos have their "arousal setting" set too high.
claims.passage: people like them, raised in chaos, had their "arousal setting" set "way too fucking high."
claims.inference: Attributed to Shepard by turn context in the medium re-transcription ("'Cause our arousal setting was set way too fucking high"). Presented as the alternative explanation.
claims.alternative: Shepard is a host in recovery with his own frame; it is a trauma reading, not a type reading.

claims.claim: In 2016 he was charged with battery on a police officer; by his account he knocked down an officer he thought had drawn a gun (later: a taser) while the officer chased his younger brother.
claims.passage: In 2016 Fike was charged with battery on a police officer. By his account, an officer was chasing his younger brother, Fike thought the officer had drawn a gun (in 2025 he said it was a taser), and he knocked the man down.
claims.inference: GQ dates the charge to 2016 and gives the plea and house-arrest sentence; NME gives the jail and April 2018 release. The incident itself rests on his account. In 2025 he described the act as reflex: 'Immediately my instinct, boom.'
claims.alternative: The account is his alone; no police record was opened. Interviewers' paraphrases vary ('punched a cop' in Blackbird; 'assaulting' in GQ). The protective impulse toward his brother is better evidence of loyalty (6, 8, 2) than of a Seven motive. Length of the custody varies by telling ('a year'); use 'months' or 'about a year' with attribution.

claims.claim: He described his reaction as reflex: "Immediately my instinct, boom."
claims.passage: "Immediately my instinct, boom," he told Shepard.
claims.inference: Armchair Expert 00:38:26 (Whisper small transcript), inside his own narration of the chase.
claims.alternative: Not re-transcribed with the medium model.

claims.claim: He pleaded guilty and was sentenced to house arrest.
claims.passage: He pleaded guilty and was sentenced to house arrest
claims.inference: GQ: "After pleading guilty, he was sentenced to six months of house arrest."
claims.alternative: Length varies by account; not printed.

claims.claim: He moved into a friend's apartment with a guitar and made the Don't Forget About Me, Demos tape on house arrest.
claims.passage: He moved into a friend's apartment with a guitar and started making the tape that became _Don't Forget About Me, Demos_.
claims.inference: GQ ("moved into a friend's apartment with his guitar"); P&P and NME say the tape was recorded on house arrest.
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: On house arrest he felt "trapped all day" and bored, and used cocaine because it clears the system quickly.
claims.passage: "But I'm in a room all day, and I'm trapped all day."
claims.inference: Medium re-transcription (aeseg-bored). His causal chain runs from confinement and boredom to stimulation.
claims.alternative: Addiction explains using under confinement regardless of type; boredom is a classic relapse trigger. In 2023 he told the Standard he was high on cocaine while playing the tape back ('Oh my god, this is so good').

claims.claim: He used cocaine for its short detection window, finished the tape, failed a 7 a.m. drug test and was cuffed on the spot.
claims.passage: "So I start using everything I can that has a short span in your stream," he went on: cocaine, because he might be drug-tested. "Yeah, I'm bored." He was up using the night he finished the last song on the tape. At 7 a.m. he was called in for a test, failed it, and was cuffed on the spot. "I'd never been so in disbelief."
claims.inference: Medium re-transcriptions aeseg-bored and aeseg-jail. "That's the great thing about coke. It makes you optimistic" in the same passage is a host's line and is not printed.
claims.alternative: Addiction explains using under confinement regardless of type.

claims.claim: He served months in Collier County Jail and was released in April 2018.
claims.passage: He served months in Collier County Jail and was released in April 2018
claims.inference: NME 2020; the Guardian says a year's sentence.
claims.alternative: Length of custody varies by telling; "months" used.

claims.claim: FAQ: released from Collier County Jail in April 2018 amid a label bidding war; signed with Columbia.
claims.passage: was released from Collier County Jail in April 2018 as major labels competed to sign him; he signed with Columbia
claims.inference: NME: executives were "clamouring" by his April 2018 release; P&P: Columbia deal.
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: He reframes hardship positively; in 2022 he called jail "a year off to focus on myself."
claims.passage: 2022, to GQ: "It really was just a year off to focus on myself."
claims.inference: Six instances across 2020-2025, sober and not, in five outlets: the first move with pain is to turn it into an upside. This is the most repeated behavior in the record and the core of the Seven case.
claims.alternative: He also states the bad parts plainly when pressed: jail 'sucks, dude', the first six months 'I was not doing too well... I was sad' (Guardian 2023). Much of the positivity is comic performance in promotional settings, and recovery culture encourages gratitude framing. The 2025 'it's all great' line is followed by 'As long as you can handle it'.

claims.claim: In 2023 he described jail as "a purgatory" that "sucks," and said he was "not doing too well" in the first six months.
claims.passage: "It's more of a purgatory... It sucks, dude." Of the first six months: "I was not doing too well."
claims.inference: Shows the bad version is available to him; balances C06.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: In 2025 he said, "I had a good time in jail."
claims.passage: 2025, to Shepard: "I had a good time in jail."
claims.inference: Medium re-transcription (aeseg-jail): "It was awesome. It was great... I'm not even kidding... I had a good time in jail," followed by Shepard's response to him.
claims.alternative: Speaker attribution rests on turn context in a machine transcript without speaker labels; not checked by ear. Comic register.

claims.claim: While he was in jail, the tape went up on SoundCloud and "3 Nights" spread.
claims.passage: While he was inside, the tape went up on SoundCloud and "3 Nights" spread.
claims.inference: Guardian 2023 (manager dropped the EP on SoundCloud; 3 Nights went viral); P&P (released December 2017 while he was in jail).
claims.alternative: Accounts differ on who uploaded it (Guardian: his manager; Armchair: he did, and Reed took it down), so the draft does not say.

claims.claim: Label executives flew from California to visit him in jail; he "felt like fucking Al Capone."
claims.passage: "These dudes start flying from California to visit me in the jail," he told Shepard. "I felt like fucking Al Capone or some shit."
claims.inference: Armchair 00:45:19 (Whisper small) and 00:51:00 (medium re-transcription in the draft stage). Both inside his own narration; Shepard's preceding hypothetical is not quoted.
claims.alternative: Comic register; not checked by ear.

claims.claim: He held out for a large deal to pay his mother's lawyer: "now or never."
claims.passage: "I really needed money for her lawyer, straight up... It was like now or never," he told Pigeons & Planes, about his mother.
claims.inference: Family provision as a motive for the deal (C24).
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: He signed with Columbia for a reported $4 million.
claims.passage: He signed with Columbia for a reported $4 million, according to the Standard
claims.inference: The Standard: "for a reported $4 million"; P&P: "rumored to be valued at around $4 million."
claims.alternative: Reported, not confirmed.

claims.claim: He describes excess as his method: money used "to have the best time you can" (2023) and drugs taken "all the way there without dying" (2023).
claims.passage: "That was my relationship with money. You use it to have the best time you can. I was bouncing off the walls, man. I was really f***ing up."
claims.inference: The aim he names is the best time, the most experience, 'all the way there' — appetite for intensity rather than control or image.
claims.alternative: Addiction pharmacology and sudden wealth explain much of this without any type. The yacht anecdotes are not printed.

claims.claim: Guardian 2023: "Whatever drug I would do, I'd do too much of it... to go all the way there without dying."
claims.passage: "Whatever drug I would do, I'd do too much of it – to [the point of] a near-death, surreal experience. I just kind of thought that was how you did drugs – to go all the way there without dying."
claims.inference: Appetite for intensity in his own words.
claims.alternative: Sensitive; placed mid-article, not as hook or ending.

claims.claim: In May 2022 he told GQ he wanted to be "annoying famous" and wanted "all of it", including "the fucked-up knees."
claims.passage: "I'm not even kidding. I'm trying to get, like, annoying famous." Why? "I want those iconic pictures from back in the day. The cool stories. The fucked-up knees from all the Ecstasy. You know? I want all of it."
claims.inference: What he wants from fame is the experience and the stories, including the damage — not a curated, admired image. A Three wants the polished picture; he asks for 'the fucked-up knees'. The 2026 reversal is dated growth, not a contradiction to hide.
claims.alternative: Deadpan comedy; the GQ answer to "Why?" begins "I just think it'd be dope…" before the quoted part. A Three reading would treat it as status hunger.

claims.claim: He took mushrooms before his first Euphoria audition, laughed and made fun of the room, and did not get the part.
claims.passage: For his first audition, he told GQ, he took mushrooms: "I started peaking right when me and Barbie were reading." In his mind's eye, Sam Levinson was wearing a dress; Fike broke out laughing, started "making fun of everybody in the room," and didn't get the part.
claims.inference: GQ narrates and quotes him; "He didn't get the part."
claims.alternative: Told as comedy.

claims.claim: About a year later Levinson offered a rewritten role and a five-year contract; Fike answered "Brother, got you" while "not understanding the stakes."
claims.passage: About a year later Levinson came back with a character rewritten "with the qualities of the guy you saw show up" and a five-year contract. Fike remembers Levinson saying, "I need to know that you're not going to like fuck me on this." His answer: "Brother, got you." In the next breath he said he was "not understanding the stakes" (Armchair Expert, 2025).
claims.inference: The audition is told consistently since 2022 and treated as comedy. The 'self-defense mechanism' line is his own explanation of his nonchalance: not caring in advance protects him from failing.
claims.alternative: The "self-defense mechanism" line was not printed: no speaker break is resolvable in either transcript. The untested handshake argues against a Six's testing of authority.

claims.claim: He told Variety in 2021 he was sober during Euphoria season 2; in 2023 he said he was using during that production.
claims.passage: In September 2023 he told the Guardian, "I was using at the time, but I wasn't worried. I was more like … psyched!" Both are his words, two years apart.
claims.inference: The record shows a repeated cycle of stated control, relapse and candid retelling. Useful for the article as dated context; not type evidence in itself.
claims.alternative: Addiction is not an Enneagram type. Recovery is time-sensitive and private; the article should not characterize his current sobriety beyond his latest dated words. Sensitive: no diagnostic labels, no speculation about risk, and avoid making the withdrawal crisis a set piece.
claims.review_trigger: Any new public statement about sobriety or relapse; recheck before each refresh.

claims.claim: August 2021: he told Variety he was sober and "in overdrive."
claims.passage: he was sober and "in overdrive."
claims.inference: Variety: "Fike is now sober. 'I'm in overdrive.'"
claims.alternative: Contradicted by his 2023 account (C15); presented as dated statements.

claims.claim: July 2023: sober "a year total, but split up over like, 5 really bad relapses. But it's all good, I'm good."
claims.passage: "It's been a year total, but split up over like, 5 really bad relapses. But it's all good, I'm good."
claims.inference: Reframing of relapse (C06 pattern).
claims.alternative: Recovery language; dated.

claims.claim: July 2023, to the Standard: "I'm not on drugs now. But I'll always be a drug addict" and his addiction "made me better."
claims.passage: That same month, to the Standard: "I'm not on drugs now. But I'll always be a drug addict." And: "I wouldn't change the fact that I'm addicted to any of that shit. It's made me better."
claims.inference: Reframing of addiction.
claims.alternative: Recovery culture encourages gratitude framing.

claims.claim: September 2025: "it's all great. Cocaine's awesome. Sobriety's awesome," qualified "As long as you can handle it," and still "figuring it out."
claims.passage: In September 2025: "I decided recently, it's all great. Cocaine's awesome. Sobriety's awesome." He added, "As long as you can handle it," and said he was "still kind of to this day, like, figuring it out."
claims.inference: Medium re-transcription (aeseg-allgreat); the run continues into his own brother-and-treatment remarks, which supports attribution. Brother details not printed.
claims.alternative: Not checked by ear.

claims.claim: FAQ sobriety answer: dated statements from July 2023, September 2025 and April 2026.
claims.passage: in July 2023 he said his sobriety was "a year total, but split up over like, 5 really bad relapses," and in September 2025 that he was "still kind of to this day, like, figuring it out." In April 2026 he said, "I just don't party like that right now."
claims.inference: Only his dated words; no characterization of current sobriety.
claims.alternative: Sensitive and time-sensitive.
claims.review_trigger: Update or remove the FAQ after any new public statement about sobriety.

claims.claim: Three journalists, writing four years apart, independently described the same affect. Tasbeeh Herwees (Pigeons & Planes, 2019): 'These are facts of his life he lists with no sense of drama.' Samuel Hine (GQ, 2022): 'there's not a single difficult topic – not his family nor incarceration nor addiction – that Fike can't spin into a positive.' Richard Godwin (Standard, 2023): 'he defies any urge to shape it into a narrative of redemption.'
claims.passage: Three journalists, writing years apart, saw the same thing in him. Herwees in 2019: "no sense of drama." Samuel Hine in GQ in 2022: "there's not a single difficult topic – not his family nor incarceration nor addiction – that Fike can't spin into a positive." Richard Godwin in the Standard in 2023: "he defies any urge to shape it into a narrative of redemption."
claims.inference: Independent observers, not self-report, and the closest thing to observed behavior across time. Godwin's line sets a limit: the lightness is not a polished comeback story (an image move a Three might make) but a refusal to linger.
claims.alternative: He told Zane Lowe he is 'desensitized' to the drug world he grew up in (S09); flattened affect from early trauma, or a Nine's numbing, would also read as 'no sense of drama'. Hine's 'spin into a positive' is the writer's frame around quotes.

claims.claim: In July 2023 he called himself "so codependent on human beings" and said that alone he wanted to "be anywhere else but in my body."
claims.passage: "I'm just so codependent on human beings and I love having them around and having them to talk to."
claims.inference: Medium re-transcription (zseg-codep) confirms wording and that "I had a really hard time sitting still in my own skin" is Lowe's, not printed.
claims.alternative: 'Codependent' is therapy vocabulary and also fits Six (needing support) and Two (needing to be needed). Do not attribute 'I had a really hard time sitting still in my own skin' to him: Zane Lowe says it (S09 24:05-25:55).

claims.claim: He tied it to sobriety and living alone: "be anywhere else but in my body."
claims.passage: "so what the fuck do I do when I'm by myself? Obviously like let's get drunk and go talk to someone or go hang out with, be anywhere else but in my body."
claims.inference: Clearest first-person statement of the avoidance the Seven reading predicts (medium re-transcription).
claims.alternative: "Codependent" also fits Six or Two.

claims.claim: He said codependency often ends his relationships; in the same film he confirmed the split with Hunter Schafer and said he was "done being in relationships right now."
claims.passage: That codependency, he told Lowe, "is often the cause of like the end of my relationships." In the same July 2023 film he confirmed that his relationship with _Euphoria_ co-star Hunter Schafer, public since early 2022, was over, and said he was "done being in relationships right now."
claims.inference: First quote verified in medium re-transcription; the split confirmation and "done being in relationships right now" as reported by ELLE (S23).
claims.alternative: Relationship status changes; no later relationship is reported.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck if he speaks publicly about the relationship.

claims.claim: In August 2024 Hunter Schafer said her last relationship ended partly because she was cheated on; she did not name him in that passage, and reporting identified him.
claims.passage: that her last relationship ended partly because "I got cheated on for the first time." She did not name him in that passage; reporting identified him
claims.inference: Attributed to Schafer; included for handling, not as type evidence.
claims.alternative: Her account is an allegation about a named person; attribute it to her, give his stated reason for the split, and note no response was found. Do not name the earlier partner or repeat the 2025 detail beyond his own words. Do not speculate about which songs refer to it.
claims.review_trigger: If Fike responds publicly to Schafer's account, update attribution and add his response.

claims.claim: No public response from Fike to Schafer's account was found in the sources opened as of October 2026.
claims.passage: No public response from Fike had been found as of October 2026.
claims.inference: Absence within the opened record; not proof that no response exists.
claims.alternative: A response may exist in unopened sources.
claims.review_trigger: If Fike responds publicly to Schafer's account, add his response.

claims.claim: In April 2026 he described music as a way not to think when sad or freaked out.
claims.passage: "When you are sad it's it's really nice to not think about shit," he said in April 2026. Some people work out or watch movies, he said, but "I was making music like whenever I was freaked out about some shit."
claims.inference: Whisper small transcript 00:02:00-00:02:13, kept disfluent; songwriting as distraction, which cuts against Four.
claims.alternative: Many musicians describe flow as escape; a Nine would also use absorbing work to quiet feeling. He calls lyrics 'the only thing I feel that I have where I excel' (S10), which shows craft pride that a Four or Three reading could use.

claims.claim: He finds it "really corny" when artists post about "how emotional" a song was; Lowe called it "trying to cheat a connection" and Fike agreed.
claims.passage: He told Lowe he finds it "really corny" when artists post about how they made a song "and how emotional it was." When Lowe called that "trying to cheat a connection," Fike agreed.
claims.inference: Captions 00:03:43-00:04:12: "trying to cheat a connection" is Lowe's phrase, which Fike repeats approvingly. Attribution corrected from the research claim.
claims.alternative: Indie-rock anti-earnestness is a genre posture. His manager pushes him to post, and the 2026 rollout (a 24/7 streaming channel, S15, S16) is heavily promotional, so the self-description may not match behavior when incentives change.

claims.claim: He called Sunburn "kind of just cathartic."
claims.passage: He also called _Sunburn_ "kind of just cathartic,"
claims.inference: Captions 00:02:49-00:02:59 ("I'm not often like writing for a purpose... It's kind of just cathartic"). Counterevidence kept visible for the Four question.
claims.alternative: Auto-caption wording; in the research-stage re-transcribed range 02:00-04:30.

claims.claim: Lowe invited him to say "once and for all" that his upbringing was not what his life was about anymore.
claims.passage: Later in the film, Lowe offered him a chance to say "once and for all" that the circumstances he grew up in were not what his life was about anymore.
claims.inference: Medium re-transcription (zseg-close). The closing-chapter line was prompted by Lowe.
claims.alternative: Prompted answer.

claims.claim: "I'm done talking about it. I'm down to close that chapter of my life."
claims.passage: "I'm done talking about it. I'm down to close that chapter of my life."
claims.inference: Medium re-transcription (zseg-close).
claims.alternative: Prompted by Lowe; also a reasonable wish to stop retelling trauma in press.

claims.claim: He was 27 and "still talking about when I was like 16."
claims.passage: He was 27, he said, "and I'm still talking about when I was like 16."
claims.inference: Medium re-transcription (zseg-close).
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: He prefers fresh starts: in 2023 he said change means refreshing "your whole friend group"; in 2025 he said his favorite part of treatment is that "no one knows you" and "You're a baby again."
claims.passage: that "when you want to change, you need to refresh your whole friend group." Asked in 2025 what he likes about treatment, he said "no one knows you so you get to create this person," and: "You're a baby again. I love that part of it."
claims.inference: Fresh starts and new possibilities, repeated over six years. Fits Seven's orientation to what comes next.
claims.alternative: The 2023 line is the Los Angeles Times as reported by TheWrap (original not opened). Treatment quote from medium re-transcription (aeseg-treatment). Reinvention can also be an image move.

claims.claim: Shepard's question framed his success as a reason not to change: "your act is working."
claims.passage: when, as Shepard put it, "your act is working"?
claims.inference: Medium re-transcription (aeseg-bandaid): "Cause your act is working."
claims.alternative: Host framing from a sober host.

claims.claim: In 2025 he described his own pattern in a metaphor: success was 'like if a dude gets like a cool cut on his arm and then they put a bandaid on and the bandaid's like Transformers. I was like, what do you mean? I'm doing great... but then you take it off and there's a fucking gash in your arm... This is a temporary fix for something that I need to actually go and heal.'
claims.passage: "Well it was kind of like if a dude gets like a cool cut on his arm and then they put a band-aid on and the band-aid's like Transformers, I was like, what do you mean? I'm doing great... but then you take it off and there's a fucking gash in your arm. That's kind of what it was, all this money. This is a temporary fix for something that I need to actually go and heal."
claims.inference: Medium re-transcription (aeseg-bandaid) confirms the answer is his (it continues into his own Euphoria-set details). Spelling/punctuation normalized from the machine transcript ("bandaids like transformers"; "what it was all this money"); the ellipsis removes a repeated "transformers bandaid".
claims.alternative: The question that prompted it came from Dax Shepard, a sober host who frames addiction this way; it describes the money and acclaim of 2018-2022, not necessarily his present.

claims.claim: In July 2023 he said he has "always had a big problem with security and safety" from moving around and never having a home.
claims.passage: "I think I've always had a big problem with security and safety 'cause I've moved around so much as a kid and I never really felt like I had a home, you know?"
claims.inference: Medium re-transcription (zseg-security). Strongest Six material.
claims.alternative: The concern is anchored in concrete circumstance (homelessness, a jailed mother) and is described as easing. A Seven also seeks security when deprived; the question is the strategy used under threat, which in his case is exit and reframe (C06, C11, C12).

claims.claim: Helping others find homes is "my favorite thing in the world," which he traced to "not feeling very safe"; the "next check" mindset "has influenced decisions" but he feels "safer now."
claims.passage: he answered, "Absolutely, it's like my favorite thing in the world. But yeah, I think it comes from that, just not feeling very safe." The mindset of "having to get that next check," he said, "has influenced decisions, but we're kind of dialing it back. I feel safer now."
claims.inference: Medium re-transcription (zseg-security). Security motive plus a caretaking pleasure: supports Six (and Two).
claims.alternative: Tied to concrete deprivation and described as easing.

claims.claim: In April 2026 he described his 2018 signing as validation plus impostor syndrome, "one fucking anxiety cocktail."
claims.passage: Of his 2018 signing, he said in April 2026 that he "probably felt validated and also a bit of the imposter syndrome," which added up to "one fucking anxiety cocktail right at the top of my chest."
claims.inference: Fear is present across the record. Six, Five and Seven all sit in the head (fear) triad, so anxiety alone does not separate them; what separates them is what he does with it.
claims.alternative: Supports Six. Impostor talk also fits Three and Four, and is near-universal among artists, as Lowe says in the same exchange.

claims.claim: In 2020 he said he prefers collaborators to reach out to him, citing "my fear of rejection."
claims.passage: In 2020 he told NME he prefers collaborators to reach out to him: "Maybe it's my fear of rejection that I've got going on... I'm weird about that shit."
claims.inference: A durable trait the stereotypical Seven (easy, expansive outreach) does not predict. It fits Nine (not intruding), Six (fear of rejection) or Four.
claims.alternative: Writing alone is also craft preference and control of credit. Keep this visible in the article as behavior the leading type does not neatly explain.

claims.claim: October 2026, asked about playing a musician on screen: "I've never been the type of guy to intrude on anybody's shit... That's why I'm bad at asking girls out."
claims.passage: "I've never been the type of guy to intrude on anybody's shit. That's why I do all this shit myself. That's why I'm bad at asking girls out."

type_hypothesis.against: (1) The only family testimony points elsewhere: his mother calls him 'the most passive, quiet child... the observer', with his brother as the loud one (C23). That fits a watchful Nine, Five or Six better than the busy-child picture of Seven. (2) He names a security motive in his own words, 'a big problem with security and safety' from never having a home, says money worries 'influenced decisions', places stability 'always in another person', and his fatherhood goals are property, reputation and sobriety (C20, C19). (3) Anxiety and impostor feelings recur from 2018 to 2026 (C21). (4) Across six years he does not pursue people: 'fear of rejection', lets collaborators come to him, 'never been the type of guy to intrude', 'bad at asking girls out' (C22). (5) He has been a loyal provider and protector since 22: his mother's lawyer, a house, the brother he tripped a police officer to protect, his brother's treatment (C04, C24), and possibly a habit of 'worrying about other people' while neglecting himself (C37, attribution unconfirmed). (6) Most of the 'excess' and 'escape' evidence overlaps with addiction; escape and minimization are what addiction and childhood trauma produce in any type, and a sober host (Shepard) reads his thrill-seeking as a trauma-set arousal level (C03, C08, C15). (7) His claimed restlessness outruns his output: three albums in eight years, a 2024-2025 break, 'finicky with dates' (C10). (8) The record is mostly self-report in promotional settings by a natural comic; three journalists' observations and one filmed scene are the only non-self-report behavior evidence, and the testimony (mother, Kenny Beats, Billie Eilish, Curry Barker) is brief or praise.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 6 explains the parts of the record Seven handles worst. Safety is an explicit, recurring concern in his own words: 'I've always had a big problem with security and safety 'cause I've moved around so much as a kid and I never really felt like I had a home' (Zane Lowe, 2023), and the 'next check' mindset shaped decisions (C20). He held out for a large deal 'now or never' to pay his mother's lawyer and promised 'I'm not gonna let anyone down' (2019). Loyalty is his most consistent virtue: to his mother, his brother, his childhood friends (he hired one as his chef), and to one manager since 2018, whom he asks to overrule him ('Don't listen to me. I'm manipulative!') (C24; S04, S11). He reports anxiety, impostor fear ('eventually people are going to figure out this like ruse'), nerves before sessions and overthinking (C21); he fears rejection and won't approach people (C22); he wants 'an older mentor' and says he is 'codependent on human beings' (C12, S09). His suspicion of men and male authority after abusive stepfathers (S06, S04, S11), his counterphobic act of knocking down an officer he thought had drawn a gun on his brother (C04), and his defiance of Naples' 'old white dudes' with face tattoos (C33) fit a counterphobic Six. Fatherhood has turned his goals toward property, reputation and stability (C19). Where Six strains: he rarely prepares, tests or doubts. He signed Levinson's five-year contract with 'Brother, got you' without grasping the stakes (C16), accepted a $4 million deal over champagne, describes the future as tiles appearing under his feet, and meets threat by leaving or joking rather than by vigilance or worst-case planning (C06, C10, C11). His security talk is tied to concrete deprivation and described as fading ('I feel safer now'). Other types tested and set aside: Nine (the quiet-observer childhood, non-intrusion, 'I'm chilling', numbing) fails on his appetite for intensity, 'I want all of it', 'all the way there without dying' and 'ride this... until the wheels fall off' (C08, C09); Four (confessional songs, impostor feeling, feeling like an 'eyesore', writing alone) fails on his refusal to dwell: he calls emotional song talk 'trying to cheat a connection', closes chapters, and found crying on command 'fucked up... horrible' (C11, C13, C14, S02); Three (wanted to 'blow up', watches metrics, 'just keeps winning') fails on his volunteered failures and his wish for messy rather than polished fame (C09, C27); Eight (excess, defiance, protecting his brother) fails on his aversion to confrontation and dominance and his deference to managers (C22; S04, S06); Two (providing for family, 'cater to other people') fails because helping is not how he describes his worth or identity, and he resists being cared for only half-jokingly (S11).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What he does when pain, threat or limitation arrives. A Six moves toward certainty and support: vigilance, preparation, testing people and authority, worst-case thinking, holding on. A Seven moves away from the pain toward stimulation and options and recasts it as fine. Across 2019-2026, eight outlets, sober and using periods, and one filmed scene, Fike does the second: he left a painful home for an adventure he wanted to be dangerous ('I wanted Alice in Wonderland', C03); used cocaine because he was 'trapped' and 'bored' on house arrest (C05); called jail 'a year off' and 'a good time' (C06); said of five relapses 'it's all good, I'm good' (C06); walked out of the motel room of his childhood after five minutes, 'this is too much, should we go to fucking beach', and swam (C11); described being alone as needing to 'be anywhere else but in my body' (C12); and used music because 'it's really nice to not think about shit' (C13). Three journalists independently saw the same reflex (C07), and he named it himself: the 'Transformers band-aid' over a 'gash' (C30). The Six reading predicts doubt and testing of the people and institutions he depends on; instead he trusts on a handshake (C16). Limit: the escape move is also what addiction and trauma produce, so the case rests on its persistence into sober periods (2023 motel and tour, 2025-2026 interviews) and on his own stated strategy, not on the drug history.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: His mother's memory of a passive, quiet, watchful child (C23); his durable reluctance to approach people, from 'fear of rejection' in 2020 to 'bad at asking girls out' in 2026 (C22); a deep, steady loyalty and provider role since age 22 that a Seven reading treats as secondary (C24); a self-deprecation ('I already know I'm a piece of shit', Armchair Expert 2025; medium re-transcription leaves unclear whether 'self-protection' was his word or Shepard's, so it is not printed) that reads as shame more than lightness; grief he describes when alone ('want to literally just scream or cry', C37) that the interviews rarely show; face-tattoo origin stories that change by telling (C33); and whether the 2026 restraint (less partying, less public exposure, fatherhood, recording what he called 'the most like professional studio album I've ever done') is a Seven's growth toward focus or a sign the security motive was primary all along. A Seven with a strong Six wing would cover some of this (codependency, anxiety, loyalty), but that is a speculative refinement, not evidence; leave the wing unknown in print.
